desc:
An m x n grid has a few blocked cells, given as a list obstacles of distinct pairs [row, col] (0-indexed, in any order). A traveller goes from the top-left cell to the bottom-right cell, moving only one step right or one step down at a time and never entering a blocked cell.

Return the number of routes modulo 1,000,000,007. The grid has up to 2.5 · 109 cells, so it cannot be filled; only the obstacles may be processed one by one. If the start or the destination is blocked the answer is 0.

m = 3, n = 3, obstacles = [[1,1]]          ->  2
m = 3, n = 3, obstacles = [[0,1],[1,0]]    ->  0
m = 2, n = 2, obstacles = []               ->  2
constraints: obstacles[i] = [row, col] with 0 ≤ row < m and 0 ≤ col < n; all pairs are distinct
hints: Without obstacles the answer is a single binomial coefficient. The difficulty is subtracting the routes that touch an obstacle without double counting.

Sort the obstacles by row, then column. For obstacle i, count the routes from the start that reach it without touching any earlier obstacle: all routes to it, minus those that first hit an earlier obstacle j.
bad[i] = W(start, i) - sum over j before i with col(j) ≤ col(i) of bad[j] · W(j, i). Treat the destination as one more obstacle placed last; bad of it is the answer. Use factorial tables for W.
editorial: Let W(a, b) be the number of unrestricted right/down routes from cell a to cell b, a binomial coefficient (0 if b is not weakly below and to the right of a). Sort the obstacles by (row, column) and append the destination as a final pseudo-obstacle. Define f[i] as the number of routes from the start to obstacle i that touch no other obstacle before reaching it.

Every route from the start to i either touches no earlier obstacle, or has a unique first obstacle j on it. Counting by first obstacle gives W(start, i) = f[i] + sum over j < i of f[j] · W(j, i), so f[i] = W(start, i) - sum f[j] · W(j, i). The sort guarantees that every obstacle that can lie on a route to i comes earlier. The value for the destination is the answer.
Factorials up to m + n modulo the prime cost O(m + n), and the double loop costs O(k<sup>2</sup>) for k obstacles. Memory is O(m + n + k).
